specPoints.text: explain, for a fixed amount of gas, the qualitative relationship between: • pressure and volume at constant temperature • pressure and Kelvin temperature at constant volume

primer.text: Squeeze a gas and it pushes back; heat it in a sealed box and it presses harder. This note sets out the two qualitative gas laws for a fixed sample — pressure against volume at constant temperature, and pressure against kelvin temperature at constant volume — each read straight off the kinetic model.

lessons.title: Pressure and volume at constant temperature
lessons.opening: Compress a gas slowly — temperature unchanged — and its pressure climbs. The molecules are the same, moving at the same speeds, but the shorter distances between walls mean every molecule lands hits more often.
keyPoints: At constant temperature, reducing the volume of a fixed gas raises its pressure.
At constant temperature, increasing the volume lowers the pressure.
The molecular speeds are unchanged at constant temperature; only the flight distances shrink.
Shorter flights mean more frequent wall collisions per second.
More frequent collisions deliver a greater total force per wall area — higher pressure.

low.restatement: Shrink the box and the same fast molecules bump the walls more often, so the pressure goes up. Give them more room and the collisions thin out and the pressure drops.
low.analogy: A fixed stream of shoppers forced through a narrower entrance: the door is hit more times per second even though each shopper walks at the same pace.
low.examPointer: Keep the two halves of the mechanism separate: same speeds (constant temperature) but more frequent collisions (smaller volume). Missing either half costs the mark.

medium.restatement: With temperature fixed, the mean molecular kinetic energy is fixed, so the impulse per collision is unchanged. Halving the volume shortens the mean free path, raising the collision rate per unit wall area; since pressure is impulse flux, it doubles in the ideal case — the inverse proportionality that Boyle quantifies.
medium.analogy: Crumpling the corridors of an office block: the walkers keep their pace, but everyone reaches an end-wall sooner, so the doors take a pounding.
medium.examPointer: The compression must be slow for 'constant temperature' to hold — a fast squeeze does work on the gas and warms it, which is why the question says 'at constant temperature'.

check.stem: A fixed mass of gas is compressed slowly at constant temperature. What happens to its pressure?

options.text: it increases
options.explanation: Smaller volume means more frequent wall collisions.

options.text: it decreases
options.explanation: Compression raises pressure.

options.text: it stays the same
options.explanation: The collision rate changes with volume.

options.text: it falls to zero when compressed
options.explanation: Compression concentrates impacts; it never empties them.

check.stem: At constant temperature, why does a larger volume give a lower pressure?

options.text: molecules take longer between wall hits, so collisions per second fall
options.explanation: Longer flight paths thin out the bombardment.

options.text: the molecules slow down in a bigger box
options.explanation: At constant temperature the speeds are unchanged.

options.text: some molecules leave the gas
options.explanation: The sample is fixed — nothing escapes.

options.text: the walls get softer
options.explanation: Wall properties do not enter the gas law.

check.stem: What is held constant for the pressure–volume relationship to apply as stated?

options.text: temperature and the amount of gas
options.explanation: Fixed sample at fixed temperature — the stated conditions.

options.text: pressure and temperature
options.explanation: Pressure is the very thing changing.

options.text: volume and temperature
options.explanation: Volume is the other variable.

options.text: nothing needs to be constant
options.explanation: The relationship is conditional on both constants.

check.stem: A balloon is placed inside a vacuum chamber and the outside pressure is gradually removed. What happens to the balloon and why?

options.text: it expands, because the trapped gas spreads into a larger effective volume at lower opposing pressure
options.explanation: Less outside squeeze lets the gas's internal pressure expand it.

options.text: it shrinks, because the gas loses molecules
options.explanation: The balloon stays sealed.

options.text: it stays the same size because gas volume is fixed
options.explanation: Gas volume is not fixed — that is the point of the law.

options.text: it freezes solid
options.explanation: Nothing in the setup cools it.

check.stem: A student compresses a gas very quickly and observes the pressure rise more than expected. What extra effect crept in?

options.text: the fast compression did work on the gas and raised its temperature, adding a second pressure rise
options.explanation: Beyond the volume effect, hotter molecules hit harder — the constant-temperature assumption broke.

options.text: the molecules multiplied during compression
options.explanation: Molecules are conserved.

options.text: the gauge always over-reads on fast changes
options.explanation: The excess is physics, not instrument error.

options.text: the volume fell below zero
options.explanation: Volumes stay positive.

check.stem: State what happens to the pressure of a fixed gas at constant temperature when its volume is halved.
check.modelAnswer: The pressure rises — in the ideal case it doubles — because the same molecules collide with the walls more frequently in the smaller volume.

check.stem: State the two conditions that must hold when relating pressure and volume of a fixed gas.
check.modelAnswer: The temperature must be constant and the amount of gas must be fixed.

check.stem: Explain, using the kinetic model, why the pressure of a gas falls as it is slowly expanded at constant temperature.
check.modelAnswer: The molecules keep the same average speeds because the temperature is unchanged, so each collision delivers the same impulse. But in the larger volume each molecule travels further between wall impacts, so each wall receives fewer collisions per second. The total impulse per unit area per second — the pressure — therefore falls.

check.stem: A vacuum pump removes air from around a sealed balloon, which swells to twice its size. Sketch the reasoning linking the change in available volume to the change in the trapped gas's pressure.
check.modelAnswer: As the outside squeeze falls, the trapped gas expands into a larger volume at the same temperature. With longer flight paths between wall hits, the internal collision rate per unit area falls, so the internal pressure drops until it balances the reduced outside pressure — the pressure falls as the volume grows.

lessons.title: Pressure and kelvin temperature at constant volume
lessons.opening: Heat a sealed, rigid container of gas and the pressure climbs on the gauge. The molecules are already fast; warmer still, they fly faster, strike harder, and return sooner — a triple intensification of the bombardment.
keyPoints: At constant volume, raising the kelvin temperature raises the pressure of a fixed gas.
Hotter molecules have higher average kinetic energy and higher average speeds.
Faster molecules deliver a larger impulse at each wall collision.
Faster molecules also return to the walls sooner, so collisions are more frequent.
Together the harder and more frequent impacts raise the pressure.

low.restatement: In a rigid sealed box, heating makes the molecules faster, so they smack the walls harder and come back for another hit sooner. Both effects push the pressure up together.
low.analogy: Hail upgrading from gravel to golf balls arriving twice as often: the roof feels it on both counts.
low.examPointer: Quote both changes — harder hits AND more frequent hits — because a one-cause answer scores half.

medium.restatement: At fixed volume the number density is fixed, so the collision frequency rises only through speed. Mean impulse per collision grows with molecular speed and the round-trip time to a wall falls with it, so the impulse flux — pressure — is proportional to mean kinetic energy, which is proportional to kelvin temperature: the qualitative seed of the pressure law.
medium.analogy: Shortening a squash court and speeding up the players simultaneously: the walls take a double penalty, pace and frequency compounding.
medium.examPointer: Connect to proportionality: pressure rises in step with kelvin temperature at constant volume — the statement the next note quantifies.

check.stem: A sealed rigid canister of gas is heated. What happens to the pressure inside?

options.text: it increases
options.explanation: Hotter molecules hit harder and more often.

options.text: it decreases
options.explanation: Heating intensifies the bombardment.

options.text: it stays the same because the volume is fixed
options.explanation: Fixed volume fixes the density, not the impact energy.

options.text: it depends on the can's colour
options.explanation: Colour is irrelevant here.

check.stem: Why do hotter molecules raise the pressure in a fixed volume?

options.text: they hit the walls harder and more frequently
options.explanation: Both the impulse per hit and the hit rate rise.

options.text: they hit the walls less often but harder
options.explanation: Faster molecules also return sooner — frequency rises too.

options.text: they become heavier
options.explanation: Mass is unchanged by heating.

options.text: they stick to the walls longer
options.explanation: Model collisions are instantaneous.

check.stem: Which quantity must be constant for the pressure–temperature relationship as stated?

options.text: the volume and the amount of gas
options.explanation: Fixed rigid box, fixed sample.

options.text: the pressure
options.explanation: Pressure is the responding variable.

options.text: the temperature
options.explanation: Temperature is the manipulated variable.

options.text: the wall material
options.explanation: Material does not feature in the law.

check.stem: A full aerosol can is thrown onto a bonfire and its internal pressure climbs. What is the most likely outcome, and which law explains it?

options.text: it bursts, because pressure rises with temperature at fixed volume
options.explanation: The sealed can is a constant-volume gas box; the fire raises T and P.

options.text: it cools down, because pressure and temperature are inversely related
options.explanation: At fixed volume the relation is direct.

options.text: nothing happens because the can is sealed
options.explanation: Sealed is exactly the risk — nowhere for the pressure to go.

options.text: the can's volume doubles to relieve the pressure
options.explanation: Rigid cans barely change volume before bursting.

check.stem: A gas at 200 K in a rigid box is warmed until the pressure doubles. What temperature has been reached, qualitatively using the proportionality?

options.text: about 400 K, since pressure tracks kelvin temperature at fixed volume
options.explanation: Doubling pressure needs doubling kelvin temperature.

options.text: about 100 K
options.explanation: Halving the temperature would halve the pressure.

options.text: 200 K still
options.explanation: The pressure changed, so the temperature did.

options.text: about 473 K
options.explanation: That adds 273 instead of doubling the kelvin value.

check.stem: State what happens to the pressure of a fixed gas at constant volume when its kelvin temperature is increased.
check.modelAnswer: The pressure increases in step with the kelvin temperature, because faster molecules strike the walls harder and more often.

check.stem: State the two ways in which faster molecules intensify the wall bombardment.
check.modelAnswer: Each collision delivers a larger impulse, and the molecules return to the walls sooner so collisions happen more frequently.

check.stem: Explain why the pressure–temperature relationship requires the amount of gas to be fixed.
check.modelAnswer: Pressure is produced by the total bombardment of all the molecules present. Adding or removing molecules changes the number of impactors independently of temperature, so the clean correspondence between kelvin temperature and pressure would be broken. Fixing the amount of gas isolates temperature as the only driver of the collision totals.

check.stem: A rigid gas cylinder left in direct sun warms from 300 K to 330 K. Using the qualitative proportionality, state roughly how the internal pressure changes.
check.modelAnswer: At fixed volume pressure tracks kelvin temperature, so the pressure rises by about a tenth — roughly 10% higher — because 330 K is 10% above 300 K.

glossary.definition: A sealed sample whose molecule count does not change during the process.
A sealed container whose volume cannot change, the setting of the pressure–temperature relationship.
The number of wall impacts per second delivering the gas's pressure.
